title: What time is the 2026 Singapore GP and how can I watch it?
excerpt:
Formula 1 moves onto Singapore for the final stop in a triple header, with the Marina Bay Street Circuit set to host Round 17 of the 2026 season – and here are the global start times for Sunday’s race.

George Russell’s title hopes suffered another blow as he retired from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, enabling team mate Kimi Antonelli to extend his lead in the drivers’ standings to a commanding 84 points. But even he couldn’t match Max Verstappen, who clinched victory for the first time this year – will he be able to repeat the feat in Singapore, or will Antonelli return to the top?

Head to the RACE HUB or scroll down for more on how and when you can watch the action, along with the global start times for each session.

What time is the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix?

Singapore will hold the final Sprint of the season, which means drivers will only have one hour of Free Practice to find their rhythm at the track. That will begin at 1630 local time on Friday, 9 October before Sprint Qualifying follows at 2030.

The Sprint gets underway at 1700 on Saturday, 10 October ahead of Qualifying under the lights at 2100, while the Grand Prix itself takes place at 2000 on Sunday, 11 October.

Check out the image below to find all the global start times for Sunday’s race.

How can I watch the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix?

You can enjoy coverage from every session live on F1 TV Pro (available in selected countries), which brings fans closer to the action via exclusive features like onboard cameras on all 22 of the drivers’ cars, and access to both Pre-Race and Post-Race Shows.

F1 TV Pro can be streamed easily via Apple TV, Chromecast Generation 2 and above, Android TV, Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Roku. F1 TV Pro is free of ad breaks and available with commentary in six languages.

Fans can also watch via F1 TV Premium, a premier service that invites fans to step into the heart of the action with the ability to watch races in 4K Ultra HD/HDR on up to six different devices, as well as a personalised Multiview feature available on select devices with 26 different feeds to choose from.

Viewers can watch every F1 Grand Prix, F1 Sprint, Qualifying and practice session live in 4K Ultra HD/HDR at home, with F2, F3, F1 ACADEMY and Porsche Supercup sessions also available to watch live on the platform.

Alternatively, live timing will be available on F1.com and the F1 app across every session during the Grand Prix weekend.

Where is the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix taking place?

Since making its debut in 2008, the Marina Bay Street Circuit has hosted every edition of the Singapore Grand Prix and delivered some of the most dramatic street races in recent memory.

The bulk of the action takes place at night against the stunning backdrop of the city skyline, but the temperatures and humidity barely go down despite the timing, making it one of the most physically demanding events of the season.

It’s been the site of both heartbreak and triumph, with Sebastian Vettel winning a record five times between 2011 and 2019.

What is the weather forecast in Singapore?

Conditions are currently expected to be very warm and humid, with temperatures reaching 32 Celsius. There’s a chance of rain across Friday and Saturday which could impact driving conditions, but no precipitation is forecast for Sunday’s Grand Prix.

title: Can Red Bull keep up their momentum after Verstappen’s Sepang win?
excerpt:
Max Verstappen finally netted a 2026 victory with a dominant drive in Sepang. With the way that he’s been driving this year it seemed inevitable that the Dutchman would hit the top step at some point this season, but I didn’t expect it to come in as dominant fashion as we eventually saw.

Max had such a stranglehold on Qualifying, topping each part of it before posting two laps good enough for pole. His dominance on Saturday was enough that some of his nearest competitors at the front expected him to runaway and hide in the Grand Prix.

This performance begs the question: where has Red Bull’s pace come from?

title: Who impressed our judges at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia?
excerpt:
Max Verstappen delivered a masterclass as he and Red Bull returned to winning ways at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. But who else impressed our Power Rankings judges at the Sepang International Circuit? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below...

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

Verstappen, Red Bull and their all-new power unit have scored a solid number of podiums over the first 15 rounds of the season, but pole position and victory had eluded them. That was until last weekend at Sepang, where the Dutchman – making good use of recent updates – stormed his way to P1 on the grid and then mastered the mixed conditions on Sunday to bag a breakthrough win. Our judges were unanimous in giving him 10/10 scores.

Aston Martin and Honda’s 2026 problems have been very well documented, but the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia marked a big step in the right direction for the new partnership. After securing a best grid slot of the campaign so far in P12, Fernando Alonso used all of his experience on a wet/dry race day to come away with a superb P8 finish.

It looked like it had all gone wrong for Lewis Hamilton and Ferrari at the start of Sunday’s race, with P2 on the grid becoming P17 at the end of the first racing lap after a gamble to start on slick tyres backfired. However, the seven-time World Champion came back fighting as the track dried out, displaying rapid pace and pulling off a series of fine moves – passing Isack Hadjar for the final podium spot in the closing stages.

While Hamilton tumbled down the order on the first lap, intermediate-shod Liam Lawson charged his way from 11th to fourth. He enjoyed wheel-to-wheel moments with Verstappen’s Red Bull, before understandably losing touch with the front-runners as conditions moved from damp to dry. Still, seventh place marked a great reward, and another boost for Racing Bulls in their battle for P5 in the standings with Alpine.

Mercedes faced a headache at Sepang as they tried to understand a host of car updates on a hot, demanding track surface. Kimi Antonelli salvaged fourth in Qualifying, which became third thanks to Hadjar’s engine-related penalty, before charging into the lead at the start and then settling for second behind Verstappen. The personal struggles of Azerbaijan behind him, Antonelli was already set to gain points over George Russell when his team mate ground to a halt late on – boosting the Italian’s championship lead to 84 points.

Hadjar impressed plenty of paddock figures when he returned to action from a wrist injury on the streets of Baku and bagged a podium finish. His strong form continued over the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia weekend, bringing third in Qualifying (before his penalty) and the potential for another rostrum in the tricky, wet/dry conditions. A slight drop in pace over the second half of the race allowed the two Ferraris through, but fifth still represented a very solid result.

Arvid Lindblad faced a massive recovery drive at Sepang after taking on new power unit elements and dropping to the very back of the grid. Remarkably, the Racing Bulls rookie made up 13 places on the first racing lap alone, putting him firmly in the mix for a points finish. After the transition from intermediates to slicks, Safety Cars, race restarts and more, a late move on Nico Hulkenberg earned himself and Racing Bulls another important point.

Speaking of Hulkenberg, the German had done plenty of things right on Sunday to rise from 15th on the grid to the points-paying positions. Unfortunately for the Audi driver, who has narrowly missed out on a reward plenty of times this season, Lindblad and McLaren’s Lando Norris – after his off-track excursion behind the Safety Car – both managed to sneak past in the closing laps and deny him.

Esteban Ocon announced that he will be leaving Haas at the end of the 2026 season in the build-up to last weekend’s event. Starting 17th, just behind team mate Ollie Bearman, he was another driver to make a sensational start to the race, climbing all the way to P7 and remaining in the top 10 over the first half. His and the team’s pace faded as conditions got drier, but the Frenchman offered another glimpse of what he can do.

Carlos Sainz also made up a hatful of positions on the first racing lap, turning 13th (after another Q2 appearance) into sixth. He remained in the battle for points as the race developed, only to be tipped into a spin by Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto exiting Turn 2. Given the drying conditions, that effectively ended his chances of scoring points there and then.

Missing out

Just missing out on the top 10 of this week’s Power Rankings list are Lance Stroll, who also displayed encouraging pace for Aston Martin, as well as McLaren driver Oscar Piastri (who finished P6) and the aforementioned Russell (who had been on course for a podium).

title: Why didn't Mercedes' upgrades provide a boost in Malaysia?
excerpt:
Mercedes’ first big upgrade since the Canadian Grand Prix over three months ago did not bring the hoped-for boost in performance around Sepang and the team are currently deep-diving into the data to understand why.

The specification change was targeted at improving medium-high speed downforce, where the car had fallen steadily further behind its rivals in recent races. To achieve this aim, the whole mass of the bodywork has been brought forwards to create more free volume ahead of the rear wheels. This has entailed moving the cooling channels to create ‘cannons’ between the sidepods and engine cover.

title: How an unexpected battle for P6 in Malaysia fell apart
excerpt:
Formula 1’s midfield is so closely matched that points are hard to come by, and any top-10 finish counts as a real achievement.

So when factors such as rain throw a curve ball and create opportunities, it’s essential for those teams and their drivers to get everything right and take full advantage.

For Carlos Sainz, Alex Albon and Esteban Ocon the early stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia promised much as they made the right tyre calls and did the job on track to charge into the top eight. However, in the end, all three were to be left disappointed.

Ocon was one of the drivers who hit problems at the original start attempt, but having been given a second chance he and Haas got it right by opting for intermediates for the start as the team split its two cars. Williams also made the optimum call by putting both drivers on inters.

On the first lap it was almost like a video game for all three, as they picked their way past those ahead who had started on slicks. At the end of the lap Sainz was P6 (from 13th), Albon P7 (from 18th) and Ocon P8 (from 17th). The Haas driver was flying, and he soon made his way past both FW48s to claim P6.

At that stage – and with the slick runners falling far behind – it was looking good for all three, but the fun was not to last.

Albon was running behind Sainz when the first Safety Car sent the field into the pits for slicks, and he lost places while double-stacked behind his team mate.

At the restart Sainz was nudged into a spin at Turn 2 by Gabriel Bortoleto. With faster cars that started on slicks gaining ground under the Safety Car both Williams drivers tumbled down the order, with Albon also fighting brake problems. Sainz had to settle for P17 at the flag.

“We were having the race and doing everything right to score a point or two today,” said the Spaniard. “But then the race went away from us, obviously with the touch with Gabi taking us off. Even though I left the space, I don’t think he expected the inside of Turn 2 to be wet, and he just bumped into me.

“It was dry from there on, and it's not like our pace was amazing. Our pit stops were also not good. So it would have been a difficult day anyway.

“We would have needed to execute a perfect race, and we had two very slow pit stops. And the execution of the race from there onwards wasn't great either. I don't know if that bump from Gabi threw us off a bit as a team, but from there it was a bit scrappy, to be honest.”

To add insult to injury, Albon didn’t even see the flag due to a late gearbox problem.

“I lost out on the double stack,” he said. “We had to box early because I flat-spotted my soft tyres with the brake issue. So then it just felt like it fell away from us. The performance was nowhere, but also nowhere on my side as well.

“Unfortunately, you just want a smooth weekend, a feeling of progress, but we've had issues with parts this weekend. Not lack of parts, just performing parts, and unfortunately, if you're not on the one part that you have, you use your second best stuff, it's not good enough, and you're immediately on the back foot. And I was on the back foot massively all weekend.”

How Alonso and Aston Martin took their opportunity in Sepang

In contrast to the two Williams drivers, Ocon survived the first Safety Car period in good shape, and still in P6.

He lost a place to the flying Lewis Hamilton, but was still P7 when he made a relatively early second stop.

Others who hung on for a later stop benefited from the second Safety Car, triggered by Albon. Points thus slipped out of his hands, and he finished P15.

“We took the right tyre for the start, I decided to stay on the inter, which was the right thing,” said the Frenchman. “We had a mega first lap on the inter, I was overtaking cars. I was up to P6. It was really good. And then from the first time we boxed, we started moving rearwards.

“So we need to exactly see what happened, but we deserved more today. We had new tyres in stock. We also boxed to used tyres at the end, and we missed the last Safety Car also.

“So 100% the start of the race, 0% at the end part of the race, of success. A bit of mixed emotion, but super sad for the whole team that has worked super hard to get this car to where it was, because it was healthy, it was working well.

“We had great pace on the soft tyre in the beginning and on the inter, and we should have been fighting for the points, and we were there. So very disappointed. But it's our fault – so we'll keep working on it.”

title: Audi unpick eventful weekend amid penalty and last-lap drama
excerpt:
The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia proved to be a particularly eventful weekend for Audi, with the squad left to reflect on a “frustrating” end to Sunday’s race that saw them lose out on points during the last lap.

After progressing to Q3 in Saturday’s Qualifying, Gabriel Bortoleto lined up in P10 on the grid while team mate Nico Hulkenberg started from P15 – but both looked set for a tough start to the race when they bolted on soft tyres, a decision that quickly went against them given the still damp conditions from the heavy rainfall that had delayed the event getting underway.

Following an early stop for the intermediates, the Audis were each able to make gains. However, Bortoleto’s progress faltered when he made contact with the Williams of Carlos Sainz, an incident that the Brazilian subsequently received a 10-second time penalty for.

Hulkenberg, meanwhile, remained in the fight for points until the very end of the race and only just missed out after being overtaken by Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad on the final lap of the Grand Prix.

Furthermore, the team were handed a fine (part of which was suspended for 12 months on the condition that there is not a similar incident in that time) for an unsafe release of Hulkenberg during a pit stop.

While he had also seen a point slip away during the final stages of the race one week earlier in Azerbaijan, Hulkenberg was pragmatic about experiencing a similar fate at Sepang.

“Obviously a few times now I just missed out, but ultimately [it was] not quite good enough, our package here,” the German explained. “That's why we couldn't hang on to that point in the end, but obviously if we're honest we only got there because of some retirements and some trouble at the front.

“I feel like it was always a long shot, but I’m much happier with my performance compared to yesterday, which wasn't so difficult, but a clean race from my side. Yeah, good racing and a good afternoon.”

On the other side of the garage, Bortoleto took the blame for his collision with Sainz after what proved to be a tough afternoon in Malaysia.

“First I want to apologise to Carlos,” said Bortoleto. “I ended up touching him there and maybe destroyed his race, a bit of mine as well, created damage in my car, and after that we were just too far behind to fight for anything.

“I was racing on my own and unfortunately had another few issues through the race as well that was very difficult to manage, but anyway, I was already gone after my contact. So I apologise to him, to my team, to his team, and we move to Singapore.“

The 21-year-old still felt that there were “a lot of positives” to take forward, adding: “I think we delivered a good upgrade in Baku and it showed to be strong here. And yeah, heads up to Singapore. I'm excited for the weekend, and hopefully we can have a good one there.”

Audi’s Racing Director Allan McNish echoed that positivity, having praised the performance of the car in Malaysia whilst acknowledging that missing out on points was a frustrating end to the event.

“We got the pace of the car. That was quite clear when we got to Qualifying,” McNish reflected after the race. “I think we had got it into the right window, and Gabi delivered a really good Qualifying.

“Nico was on a similar pace till Turn 14. These things happen. And I think, we sort of got back through to roughly that point by the end of the race. Not quite that same point, but very close to it.

“So in terms of that, yeah, it was a bit frustrating to be overtaken in the last lap again, because that's two races consecutively where we've been done in the last lap and that's a little bit frustrating. But I think we know where our strengths and weaknesses are and we know we're a bit exposed, and when the Safety Car came out we become a bit more exposed.”

title: FIA Formula 2 and FIA Formula 3 announce 2027 calendars
excerpt:
The FIA Formula 2 Championship and FIA Formula 3 Championship have announced their respective calendars for the 2027 campaign.

Both junior single-seater championships will continue to support Formula 1 across the 2027 season, with F2 featuring at 14 rounds, while Formula 3 will be present at 10 rounds next year alongside both.

F2 returns to Montreal after racing in Canada for the first time in 2026, while Mexico City joins the calendar for the first time. Istanbul will also feature on the calendar as a new venue, staging a race for the first time in the FIA Formula 2 era.

Formula 3 will visit Jeddah and Montreal for the first time, while the season finale will take place at another new venue in Istanbul.

Both championships will begin their campaigns in March in Bahrain and Jeddah before heading to Melbourne in April and Montreal in May.

F2 and F3 then return to action in June around Monaco before back-to-back rounds at Silverstone and Spielberg.

Following the summer break, both championships resume racing in Monza before heading to Madrid.

F2 is the sole supporting championship in Azerbaijan in September, before both join F1 in Istanbul for what will be the season-ending F3 round.

F2 visits Mexico at the end of October before going to Qatar and Abu Dhabi for the final two rounds of the campaign.

Stefano Domenicali, President and CEO of Formula 1 said: “The 2027 FIA Formula 2 calendar will deliver another exciting season of racing across 14 rounds at some of the most iconic and challenging venues in world motorsport, including the addition of Istanbul and Mexico City.

“Formula 2 continues to play a vital role as the ultimate pathway to Formula 1, giving the most promising young drivers the opportunity to compete on the same stage as the pinnacle of our sport and showcase their talent to fans, teams and partners around the world. Year after year, the championship delivers outstanding racing and helps develop the next generation of Formula 1 stars.

"“I would like to thank the FIA President and their entire team, Bruno Michel and his team, as well as all our promoters, partners, officials, marshals and volunteers whose dedication and commitment make this Championship possible. I look forward to following another highly competitive season in 2027.”

Bruno Michel, FIA Formula 2 CEO said: “I’m very excited to add three new venues in a financially sustainable way, with the return of Montreal following its surprise addition in 2026 and the first appearance of Istanbul and Mexico City.

“We will be covering freight costs so that the territorial expansion of the calendar does not financially impact our teams.

“With a calendar spanning four continents and a carefully distributed sequence of rounds, the 2027 FIA Formula 2 Championship will offer teams and drivers a demanding and diverse season, while bringing the category to new audiences and strengthening its position as a global platform for the next generation of Formula 1 talent.”

title: Red Bull disclose further details of successful Max Verstappen negotiations
excerpt:
Max Verstappen re-signed with Red Bull over the summer. Now, team principal Laurent Mekies has shared some of the main themes of those negotiations.

Red Bull's recent run of upgrades was not a decisive factor in convincing Max Verstappen to extend his contract until 2030, Laurent Mekies has revealed.

Instead, the Red Bull team principal has insisted the team's long-term development direction mattered far more than any single update during negotiations.

Verstappen committed his future to Red Bull in August, ending months of speculation that had included interest from McLaren after Mercedes' pursuit of the four-time F1 drivers' champion cooled.

The Dutchman had even entertained the possibility of walking away from Formula 1 altogether before signing fresh terms with the Milton Keynes-based squad, and suggested he was closer to retirement than joining a rival team.

Those talks took place against a backdrop of a difficult start to the RB22's campaign, with Red Bull well off the pace in the opening rounds before incrementally closing the gap.

That progress culminated in Verstappen fighting for victory on merit at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, where he finished just two tenths of a second behind winner George Russell, before taking a maiden win of the campaign at the following round at the Sepang International Circuit.

Asked whether Red Bull knew its recent upgrades would deliver the gains they have, and whether that influenced the negotiations with Verstappen, Mekies told media, including RacingNews365: "The short answer is no.

"We were not waiting for a magic upgrade that was supposed to come and bring us to the performance."

Mekies reveals true nature of Verstappen negotiations

Speaking after Verstappen and Red Bull triumphed at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Mekies explained that the Baku upgrade, since followed by a revised floor board geometry for Sepang, was always understood internally as the final piece of that development cycle rather than a surprise breakthrough.

"We knew we had upgrades," the Frenchman continued. "We actually knew that Baku would be the last one. It was continuing the trend of the development of the car.

"Actually, at the time [of the discussions with Verstappen], we felt we would probably struggle to close those final three tenths. So it was certainly not an argument of negotiation or convincing at the time of the discussions."

Instead, Mekies said the conversations with Verstappen centred on the broader trajectory of Red Bull's chassis and power unit departments, the latter still in its early stages as a Ford-backed in-house project.

"But I think more globally, we more so knew the dynamic was very, very strong in Pierre's [Pierre Wache, technical director] team and in Ben's [Ben Hodgkinson, technical director of Red Bull Powertrains] teams, in terms of what we felt was still the potential of the car package, chassis side and power unit side," Mekies added.

"And yes, those were the sort of discussions we had with Max; not about the Baku package or any other package, but about the underlying work happening in Pierre's team and in Ben's team, and where we felt there were lap time opportunities and long-term opportunities, but nothing specific to the Baku package."

title: Lewis Hamilton issues forceful Ferrari instruction amid rampant F1 speculation
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has told his Ferrari rank-and-file "not to read any of the stuff being written" amid the rampant speculation around the future of boss Fred Vasseur.

Vasseur's future at the helm of the Scuderia has been called into question in the past few weeks, with former Red Bull boss Christian Horner issuing a 'come-and-get-me-plea' to the team by declaring it to be the "dream job" in F1.

Horner also made clear that Ferrari was the only job he would consider in F1 where he would stay as an employee of a team rather than join the ownership structure, something he is keen to do as he seeks a route back into grand prix racing following his 2025 dismissal as CEO and team principal of Red Bull.

Reacting to the rumours for the first time, Vasseur claimed the Horner links were distracting the "serenity" within Ferrari - with the team setting up an extraordinary media briefing between the Azerbaijan and Bahrain races to confirm chairman John Elkann and CEO Benedetto Vigna enjoyed "full confidence" in the Frenchman, who has been in control since replacing Mattia Binotto ahead of the 2023 season.

Whilst Hamilton himself feels the rumours have "zero effect" on him, he felt the same could not be said for the mechanics and engineers on the shop floor - as he issued a firm instruction.

"For me, I don't read all the stuff, so it has zero effect on me. But of course, when I come into the room and see it, it definitely affects individuals in the team because every weekend they try to show up and do the best job they can, and they don't get it right all the time," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365.

"When your families are messaging you for things that they're reading, all the negative things that they're reading, when the people back at the factory are reading all those things, even though they're giving it their all, it's like they just can't do [anything].

"There's nothing [they can do]; it's almost like sometimes you feel there's nothing you can do right, even when you're giving it all. So, I just talk for me.

"The message is to not read any of the stuff that's being written, because the fact is nobody who's writing any of the stuff has actually any clue what they're talking about because they're not in the team. They don't know what's happening behind closed doors.

"They don't know how hard everybody's working. It's all done through assumptions and opinions. So that's just frustrating to see."

The article continues below.

Hamilton's 2027 feeling

Although Ferrari's 2026 title challenge has faltered as the season has progressed, Hamilton believes the blocks are in place for 2027.

"What we're going to do is just continue to try and focus on doing the best job we can, regardless of what's written. We will get to where we want to be," he said.

"I knew in the second year [of being in the team], we weren't going to be where we want to be, but I'm hoping and praying with the hard work of everybody, maybe next year we can get to where we want to."

title: Liam Lawson sends clear message over F1 future as decision timeline set
excerpt:
Liam Lawson does not believe there is much more he could have done this season to save his F1 seat at Racing Bulls.

Lawson has been one of the standout performers in Formula 1 this year, but there is still uncertainty over his future with the Faenza-based squad.

The New Zealander is currently 'best of the rest' in the standings in ninth, and impressed during the three rounds he deputised for Isack Hadjar at Red Bull, after the 21-year-old sustained a wrist injury while training over the summer break.

Fourteen of Lawson's 65 points came during that stint, and his results have helped vault Racing Bulls to comfortably occupy fifth in the constructors' standings, 22 points clear of closest rivals Alpine.

However, there are still no guarantees for 2027 and with highly-regarded junior Nikola Tsolov, who is in the fight for the F2 drivers' title, waiting in the wings, there is a difficult decision for Red Bull to make.

When Lawson was asked if he had an update, he told media, including RacingNews365: "At this stage, it's pretty similar to how it's been.

"There are conversations obviously constantly being had in the background, but for me, it's very much 'focus on the racing'."

Lawson to 'keep those points rolling in'

Team principal Alan Permane and CEO Peter Bayer have both voiced their satisfaction with the current line-up of Lawson and Arvid Lindblad, and have very much acknowledged that it is a good problem to have.

For Lawson, it is a case of keeping his head down and continuing to do what he has done all season.

"I don't feel like there's much more I could have done this year," the Racing Bulls driver added.

"We've had a good season, and at the moment, [we're] in a good place in the championship, and that's where I'm trying to stay.

"I'm going to try to stay in ninth and keep those points rolling in, and those decisions I'm sure will be made in the next few weeks."

title: Is Red Bull now emerging as the biggest F1 threat to Mercedes?
excerpt:
As the old adage goes, in F1, 'you are only as good as your last race.'

And for Red Bull, that means it is the best as Max Verstappen stormed to a dominant victory in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia - the team's first of the season and with its own in-house Red Bull-Ford Powertrains engine.

But is the team now emerging as the closest threat to Mercedes, the runaway championship leaders?

Since the Belgian GP, Verstappen has finished at least third in every race, bar the Netherlands, where he crashed on the opening lap in the tricky conditions, with the team 18 points behind McLaren in third and 107 behind Ferrari in second.

Mercedes, 258 points ahead, won't be caught by Red Bull, but can the Milton Keynes squad rally to finish as runners-up as its new threat emerges?

title: Cupra Kiro boss issues update on second Formula E seat situation
excerpt:
Cupra Kiro team principal Russell O'Hagan has revealed that Dan Ticktum remains in contention for the team's second Formula E race seat, despite the Briton testing for rival outfit Lola Yamaha during the off-season.

Ticktum completed a two-day private development test in Guadix, Spain, aboard Lola Yamaha's Gen4 test car, marking the first time in his Formula E career he has driven for a team other than Cupra Kiro, previously known as ERT and NIO 333.

He has also held discussions with other teams on the grid over potential race drives for the 2026-27 season, running parallel to ongoing talks over remaining with Cupra Kiro.

Pepe Marti's side of the garage is already settled. The Spaniard extended his deal with the team in September, having impressed as a rookie last season with podium finishes in Monaco and Sanya.

Who joins him remains the outstanding question as the team prepares for Formula E's new Gen4 era, which brings permanent all-wheel drive, peak power outputs of 600kW and a heavier car overall.

However, with a revamped sporting format which features more points being on offer in qualifying, drivers who excel over one-lap are highly desired. Last season, it was difficult to find a better qualifier than Ticktum.

Cupra Kiro decision 'two or three weeks away'

Speaking to RacingNews365 at Bridgestone's unveiling of its Formula E tyres in Rome last week, O'Hagan said the call is nearing its conclusion.

"Yeah, Dan's still an option," he revealed. "We've got two or three potential options, and we're getting to the point now where we're getting closer to making that decision. So probably a few weeks away, two or three weeks away until it's kind of confirmed publicly.

"But we've taken the time to make the right choice to understand exactly how the racing will play out, what the cars will look like, what driver qualities that leans into and rewards. Yeah, so getting ever closer to that."

Cupra Kiro has also held talks with current Formula 2 drivers as it weighs up whether to go with an experienced hand or a fresh face for the switch to Gen4 machinery.

Asked whether the shortlist leans towards experience or youth, O'Hagan was non-committal.

"It's a mix," O'Hagan replied. "There's no other names that we can share. I think in Formula E there's quite a high barrier for rookies typically, but as you see with any big step change in technical regulations, sometimes to come in as a rookie in the first year of a new generation can give you a benefit because obviously you're not comparing to something that's different from before.

"Yeah, so there's not as many barriers to making that selection as there would normally be. It's going to come down to talent and making the right choice. So, in a few weeks' time, everyone will know which way we're going."

title: Nico Hulkenberg wanted to 'eat the steering wheel' as perfect gamble ruined
excerpt:
Nico Hulkenberg was nearly the hero in the Bahrain GP - but was left "eating my steering wheel."

Nico Hulkenberg has described how he was left "eating my steering wheel" after his Bahrain GP gamble was ruined by the safety car.

As conditions improved in the Sepang race, drivers on the intermediate tyres were faced with the crossover point of when to switch over to the slick, dry tyres, with Hulkenberg pulling the trigger at the end of his eighth lap.

He emerged from the pits in 14th place, and ahead of those who had toughed the conditions out on slicks, with Lando Norris at the head of this particular train of cars.

However, Hulkenberg's gamble was then ruined by the safety car being deployed on Lap 9 for Valtteri Bottas's beached Cadillac, which then allowed those ahead on the intermediates to pit and emerge ahead of the Audi, which took the restart in 13th.

Reflecting after his 11th place finish, Hulkenberg described how he was initially feeling "like a hero" at the decision to pit.

"I was eating my steering wheel in that moment; it seriously sucked because I was feeling brave and like a hero in that moment," Hulkenberg told media, including RacingNews365.

"I made it work quite well; I made it into Turn 6, Turn 7 when the safety car came out, and it was going quite well until that moment.

"So I think we could have undercut a few people there, but unfortunately, the safety car had other plans."

The article continues below.

Hulkenberg's damage limitation

Ultimately, Hulkenberg finished in 11th place for the fourth time this season, just missing out on a points finish after late battles with Norris and the Racing Bulls machine of Arvid Lindblad.

The German had been one of the drivers to take the first standing start on the slick tyres before quickly abandoning them for intermediates before the failed safety car gamble.

"It was damage limitation, yeah, it was too ambitious to go on slicks, but this track has a history of drying up quickly, but I think the sun was missing a bit for that, so it took quite long," he said.

"But we realised and repaired the damage quite quickly, and picked up everyone on slicks within a lap or two, so it didn't cost that much; it was kind of a freebie.

"Then there was a lot of good racing, a lot of good fighting, but I don't know if the [Albon] safety car was so advantageous for us at the end.

"We didn't have enough speed to defend the position, and we were only in that position in the first place because George [Russell] and Lando [Norris had issues, so points were a long shot."

title: Oliver Bearman sends Haas clear message ahead of major team change
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman will have a new team-mate at Haas next year.

Oliver Bearman has insisted he is ready to be a team leader at Haas as he prepares for his third full season in 2027.

The Briton will enter the year with a new team-mate after Haas confirmed it would part ways with Esteban Ocon at the end of the current campaign.

While the team has not yet declared who it will sign to replace him, the heavy favourite is believed to be Brazilian Rafael Camara, who would join the grid as a rookie.

Should this be the case, Haas would lean more on Bearman to steer the development of the car with his feedback due to his extra experience.

But Bearman insists he has no concerns about doing so.

“I think that I’ve come a long way in those two years,” Bearman told media including RacingNews365

“If I compare myself to… I mean, my first few races were very unique circumstances, but even if I compare to the level that I was performing at last year, I’ve definitely come a long way.

“Especially with how I interact with the team off-track and what I understand about how to get the most out of the guys and developing the car as well.

“So, in that sense I’m looking forward to this kind of new role.”

[Article continues below]

Haas at a disadvantage?

Should this be the case, Bearman will become F1's least experienced 'lead driver' if the 2027 grid stays as it currently stands, following Esteban Ocon's departure from Haas.

Among drivers who would be considered a team's de facto number one, Liam Lawson comes closest to Bearman when it comes to being new to the role, with the Racing Bulls driver on 61 entries to Bearman's 53.

Lawson's route to that status has been shaped by Red Bull's junior program, a Super Formula stint in Japan, and reserve duties across both Red Bull Racing and the sister Faenza squad. He also deputised for Daniel Ricciardo in 2023 and for an injured Isack Hadjar at Red Bull this year.

Bearman's own path included joining the Ferrari Driver Academy in late 2021, a point-scoring emergency debut for Ferrari in Saudi Arabia in 2024, and extensive FP1 mileage with Haas before his promotion.

Haas is understood to have been steering Bearman toward a leadership role for some time, easing his transition from a junior pairing with Ocon into the team's technical reference point.

However, he remains part of the Ferrari driver academy and is seen as a future option for the Maranello-based outfit.

title: FIA explain why formation lap F1 engine bug was not previously detected
excerpt:
The FIA has explained why the software bug which affected F1 cars on the formation lap of the Bahrain Grand Prix was not previously detected.

Owing to the wet weather conditions at Sepang, the field was set for two laps behind the safety car to sight the track ahead of the race, but on the first of these, pole-sitter Max Verstappen's Red Bull slowed to a crawl, as he reported in that he could not accelerate.

Verstappen eventually got going again, but second-place starter Lewis Hamilton also slowed down and stopped on the track, with Ferrari telling him a software fix was being worked on as Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas also stopped.

The starting sequence was then suspended and the red flags brought out as the cars returned to the pit-lane, with the race then starting without further incident after FIA technicians on-site worked out a software fix and patched this to all 22 cars.

The issues arose from a wet-weather mode in the software, which is used by all teams and power unit manufacturers, that trim the power available from the full, dry-weather 350kw to 250kw in the rain in certain areas of the track.

Only when the cars were going slowly on approach to the slow, uphill left-hander of Turn 9 behind the safety car did the problems begin - with cars not having run their power units in wet-weather modes in competition in 2026.

There has been some wet weather running, including at Suzuka for Racing Bulls and Fiorano for Ferrari, but this has been in Pirelli tyre testing, with some brief instances also during pre-season testing.

Explaining why the bug had not been caught, single-seater technical director Nikolas Tombazis explained that the "combination of events" on the formation lap was not something that had been foreseen.

"I think it was a combination of the very low speeds that were far lower than you would do in testing that caused it," Tombazis told media, including RacingNews365.

"I don't believe those tests were in any way representative of the situation in order to help us catch it in time.

"Software has to be tested in more detail, and I don't know whether unfortunately or not, but this year we've had, generally speaking, very good weather, and that's the reason why it happened so late.

"Any bug is a product of a mistake. I don't know any software that doesn't have bugs and updates.

"Of course, anticipating these things is what one hopes to do, but sometimes, a combination of events isn't properly anticipated and causes the problem."

The article continues below.

'This problem will never happen again'

Reflecting, Tombazis declared that whilst any similar problems in future could not be ruled out, the specific bug which had caused the issues in Sepang would not happen again.

"I mean, cars are complicated when you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together," Tombazis added.

"Obviously, when you want to ensure sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated. So we would all like it to be simpler, but the fact is, when you have as much electrical energy, it does make it more complicated.

"After every race, we have a long debrief afterwards, where we identify criticalities.

"Obviously, that was a major criticality, and we need to make sure we avoid it.

"But can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes.

"A problem, no. But we will do our best to avoid it, of course."

title: F1 to return to Africa for brand new grand prix
excerpt:
Formula 1 is to return to racing in Africa, RacingNews365 has learned from multiple sources.

It is understood from well-placed sources in the paddock that Rwanda will be granted the opportunity to host a grand prix, with the race set to join the calendar in 2030.

According to our information, an agreement has been reached, and an official announcement could come later on this year - potentially in the coming weeks.

Rwandan President Paul Kagame has made significant efforts in recent years to secure an opportunity for his country to join the top tier of motorsport.

At Kagame’s initiative, the Rwandan capital Kigali hosted the FIA General Assemblies and Prize Giving Ceremony in 2024. Following months of speculation, Kagame used the event to announce that his country would bid to host a Formula 1 race.

As Rwanda currently has no circuit capable of hosting such an event, Kagame’s announcement was met with some scepticism within the F1 community. Nevertheless, the plans did not disappear. The president attended the 2025 Azerbaijan Grand Prix and has maintained close contact with both FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem and F1 President and CEO Stefano Domenicali.

According to information obtained by RacingNews365, it has now been decided that Rwanda will build a permanent racing circuit, based on the plans that were previously leaked.

The complex will be constructed approximately 40 kilometres from Kigali, near Bugesera International Airport, based on designs by WurzDesign.

The company belongs to former F1 driver and circuit designer Alexander Wurz and is currently working - together with Tilke Engineering - on the Qiddiya Speed Park circuit in Saudi Arabia.

F1’s return to Africa has been a longstanding topic of discussion within the series, which last raced on the continent at the 1993 South African GP at Kyalami.

Several attempts have been made in recent years to bring F1 back to Africa.

In South Africa, the former host venue Kyalami, as well as Cape Town, have sought the opportunity to host a race, while there have also been rumours about the intention of Morocco and Nigeria.

Although there is no shortage of interest in hosting grands prix around the world, prominent figures within the sport have long agreed that the African continent should return to the F1 calendar.

Among the drivers, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton has been one of the most vocal advocates for the initiative, which has also regularly received support from ben Sulayem and Domenicali.

title: Williams make third-driver change for Singapore Grand Prix weekend
excerpt:
Williams has confirmed Victor Martins will take up reserve driver duties for the Singapore Grand Prix, stepping in for Luke Browning.

Browning is absent from Marina Bay as he competes in Rounds 9 and 10 of the Super Formula Championship at Fuji Speedway, Japan, with the double-header forming the penultimate round of his campaign with Kondo Racing before the season finale at Suzuka.

Martins' call-up marks his third stint with the trackside team this season, having last fulfilled reserve duties at the Belgian Grand Prix.

The Frenchman joined the Williams driver academy in 2025 before being promoted to test and development driver this year, a role in which he has worked closely with Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz on car development and set-up work across race weekends.

Martins arrives in Singapore with a broad base of experience beyond the Williams garage. He spent three seasons racing in Formula 2 with ART Grand Prix between 2023 and 2025, picking up multiple race wins and podiums, and claimed the Anthoine Hubert Award as the series' top-placed rookie in his debut campaign.

The 24-year-old also competes in the World Endurance Championship's Hypercar class for the factory Alpine Endurance Team, sharing the No. 36 Alpine A424 LMDh alongside Jules Gounon and Frédéric Makowiecki, having made his Le Mans debut this year.

He has additionally taken part in Formula E testing with the Nissan squad, including rookie and pre-season sessions in Berlin and Madrid.

Discussing his latest reserve outing, Martins said: "It's always great to be back trackside with the Williams F1 Team as reserve driver. Being here gives me the chance to work closely with the team, and for me as a driver, it's also a great learning opportunity for my own development.

"Having been part of the Williams family since 2025, I'm looking forward to another weekend of supporting to help maximise our results."

title: Lewis Hamilton calls out hypocrisy over Iran as F1 Middle East decision looms
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has called out what he believes to be hypocrisy in relation to the status of the Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix and F1's recent trip to Azerbaijan.

The status of the Lusail and Yas Marina races remains uncertain amid the ongoing Iran War in the Middle East, with a new deadline in place by mid-October for F1 to make a decision on whether the races will take place as scheduled on the final weekend in November and first weekend in December, respectively.

It is currently understood that F1 intends to race at both venues for a 23-race season, with the only race falling by the wayside then being the Saudi Arabian GP, as the Bahrain GP was rearranged and is being held in Malaysia.

However, F1 recently raced in Azerbaijan, which shares a direct land border with Iran, something neither Qatar nor Abu Dhabi does.

Baku (around 350 miles) is also considerably closer to the Iranian capital Tehran than either Doha (around 700 miles) or Abu Dhabi (around 800 miles) as the crow flies - with Hamilton picking up on the fact that no concerns were raised around racing in Baku when asked about Imola potentially standing in to host the season-finale.

"Imola is a beautiful track to drive, but it would not be very interesting to have the last race there," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365.

"I drove there recently, and it's very bumpy when you've got [straight mode] open, and there won't be overtaking.

"I think people talk a lot about the two, and I don't know everything that is going on in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, as far as Qatar and Abu Dhabi seem okay.

"No one seems to mention that we were just in Azerbaijan, which is right next to Iran, and no one said anything about it.

"So I hope there is peace and we can go to those last two, because they're beautiful, and particularly Abu Dhabi, I really like."

title: F1 told to take 'hard look at itself' after shambolic mess
excerpt:
Williams F1 driver Carlos Sainz believes F1 should "have a hard look at itself" after the shambolic formation laps at the wet Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

For the first time at a grand prix, the new 2026 power units were run in wet conditions on Sunday at Sepang, but on the first of two formation laps behidn the safety car to evaluate track conditions, the field almost ground to a halt as cars could not accelerate.

Pole-sitter Max Verstappen nearly ground to a halt, whilst Lewis Hamilton, Esteban Ocon, and Valtteri Bottas did, with the starting procedure then suspended with the field wildly out of original grid order with Hamilton almost 'lapped' by Verstappen before he got going again.

During the red flag, the FIA quickly identified the issue and sent a software patch to all 22 cars which allowed the grand prix to go ahead without further trouble once it started.

The 2026-spec power units have often been criticised for their reliance on the beefed-up battery systems to produce 50% of their total power output, a rise from around 20% from the 2025 engines, with changes being made in both 2027 and 2028 to reduce battery reliance and increase that of the ICE.

The regulations were designed in such a way to entice new manufacturers into grand prix racing, with Audi opting to enter as a full works outfit, being unveiled at the 2022 Belgian GP, whilst Honda, General Motors/ and Red Bull-Ford have either returned to F1 as a power unit manufacturer, are planning to do so in the future or teamed up to tackle the new rules.

However, despite this, Sainz, who finished 17th in Sepang, believes questions need to be asked about who signed off on such power units.

"Well, I think Formula 1 needs to have a hard look at itself and see how we ended up in this situation," Sainz told media, including RacingNews365.

"It is clear the regulations are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the PUs, for the manufacturers, and it is too complicated switching power from dry to wet. It is too complicated.

"My only question is, who five years ago decided that this was the direction to go? Now that we are in this situation, I think we're doing the best with what we are given as a sport and the FIA and F1 are doing the best they can with what was decided five years ago.

"But clearly, what was decided four or five years ago is wrong, and [this] proves it again.

"So there is not a lot more to say. Let's learn as a sport not to make these mistakes again and not suffer from these strange cases again."

title: George Russell to start Singapore GP from back of grid after fresh penalty
excerpt:
George Russell is to start this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid after his costly power unit failure in the Bahrain GP.

Behind the safety car in Sepang, Russell pulled the Mercedes off to the side of the track with a power unit failure - the second of the season to strike the Briton following the Canadian GP.

Russell was already set to take one grid penalty in the closing stages of the season when Mercedes introduced its ADUO-boosted engine upgrade, believed to be in the United States GP in Austin.

A team spokesman has confirmed to RacingNews365 that Russell will be taking a new power unit in Singapore - and will incur the back-of-the-grid penalty.

At this stage, it is still to be confirmed if the ADUO-boosted engine could be fast-tracked into the W17 for Russell or if this new power unit he will take will be of the current specification.

If the ADUO-boosted engine is brought into Russell's pool, it would negate the need for a "double whammy" penalty of Russell taking a back-of-the-grid start for his old-spec engine, and then taking another such penalty for the ADUO upgrade.

Russell's penalty will be served in the grand prix itself on Sunday and not during the Sprint race, where he will start where he qualifies, save any in-weekend penalties for himself or other drivers, which either demote or promote him, respectively.

Team-mate Kimi Antonelli took his own batch of fresh components at the Italian GP, storming from 19th on the grid to win, although overtaking on the streets of Marina Bay is a far tougher prospect.

Following the power unit failure in Sepang, coupled with Antonelli scoring 18 points for second place, the points gap between the Mercedes team-mates opened to 84.

Antonelli cannot win the title in Singapore, with 150 points remaining after the weekend, but if he were to score a maximum of 33 points through victories in the Sprint and grand prix, with Russell not scoring a point, the Italian could be crowned world champion at the United States GP in Austin.

title: Charles Leclerc voices concern after Sepang chaos: 'It was scary'
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has stated that the on-track issues that occurred on the formation lap in Sepang were "scary" to endure.

Multiple cars came to a halt as they rounded the circuit at slow speed, with many others unable to accelerate due to a software bug with the power unit.

The FIA declared that a mix of factors caused this, including low engine speeds and wet weather management systems.

Leclerc revealed he was unsure what was happening behind the safety car, with Max Verstappen pulling a huge gap to the field after he got his own power back.

"At first I thought that the safety car had switched off the light, I couldn't see the safety car," Leclerc told media including RacingNews365.

"There was too much spray, so I thought the safety car had gone, and Max was taking the gap to warm up the tyres, which I was like, 'Okay, fine'.

"And then they told me on the radio, 'we think Max has a problem'. Then Max went, Lewis was slow, and I waited.

"At one point I was just like, 'okay, I'm probably just going to go'. And when I went on throttle, I had exactly the same problem.

"I realised everybody was in the same boat. We were stuck at like 20 km/h. It's a little bit scary to see that on a Formula 1 car."

Leclerc warns over major F1 shunt

Sunday's event marked the first time this year that the F1 cars were run in wet conditions in a competitive setting.

Leclerc has warned that the sport is risking a major shunt if power differences occur in low visibility.

"That's a bit our worry with these cars, not to that extent, of course, this was a problem, but whatever you have when you get out of the corner, sometimes you can have 100 horsepower more, 100 horsepower less," he said.

"You are not completely in control of the power you are given, and with this kind of visibility at the start of the race, you can have big shunts because of that.

"It's not the greatest cars to drive in these conditions."
